title: C# Questions & Answers - Delegates in Detail
sourceFile: Delegates in Detail - C# Multiple Choice Questions - Sanfoundry.html
description: This set of Basic C# Questions and Answers focuses on "Delegates in Detail".

questions.question: What is the correct way to instantiate and call a delegate for the method 'x' in class 'Sample'?
questions.explanation: A delegate declaration must match the signature (return type and parameters) of the method it points to. Option B correctly matches the 'void (int, double)' signature.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct way to wrap the function 'abc' into a delegate in C#?

options.text:
Csharp s = new Csharp();
delegate void d = new Del(s.abc);

questions.explanation: The delegate 'Del' must have an 'int' return type to match the 'abc' method. Option C correctly defines and invokes the delegate.

questions.question: Choose the correct syntax to call the parameterless method 'abc' using a delegate.
questions.explanation: To use a delegate, you first declare the delegate type, then create an instance of it pointing to a specific method.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code snippet?
questions.explanation: The Substring(7) starts at the 8th character (index 7). In "Test Your C#.NET Skills", index 0-3 is 'Test', 4 is space, 5-6 is 'Yo'. Index 7 is 'u'. So it results in 'ur C#.NET Skills'.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code snippet?
questions.explanation: The Replace(',', '-') method looks for commas to replace with hyphens. Since there are no commas in the input string, the string remains unchanged.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about delegates is correct regarding their implementation in .NET?

options.text: All delegate types are implicitly derived from System.MulticastDelegate
Delegates are sealed, meaning you cannot derive from a delegate type
Only the system and compilers can derive explicitly from Delegate or MulticastDelegate

questions.explanation: In C#, delegates are special classes. The compiler handles the inheritance from MulticastDelegate, and users are not allowed to manually derive from these base classes.

questions.question: Which of the following are common uses for delegates in C#?
questions.explanation: Delegates are the foundation for events, provide a way to pass methods as arguments (callbacks), and support asynchronous programming patterns.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following C# code?
questions.explanation: The method Fun replaces every occurrence of character 'k' with 'o'. Thus, 'Ykur' becomes 'Your'.

questions.question: Which of these statements about C# delegates is INCORRECT?

options.text: Delegates are used to encapsulate a method
A delegate can only ever point to one method at a time

questions.explanation: Multicast delegates can point to and invoke multiple methods in a single call using the '+' or '+=' operators.

questions.question: Which access modifiers can be applied to a delegate declaration?
questions.explanation: Since delegates are types (like classes), they support standard access modifiers to control their visibility.
